title: One teacher (Matthew 23:1–12)
hookLine: a new title on the choir list, and a teacher who says: call no one Rabbi
tomorrow: why would a speech full of woes end with a hen?

lines: A NEW TITLE ON THE DOOR.
THEN HE TURNS TO HIS OWN.
cards: The list goes up on the choir room door: a name beside every section, and a new word beside it. Leader. Titles feel good.
People screenshot them. In Matthew 23, Jesus is speaking to the crowd and to his disciples, and the subject is exactly that: how teachers like to be seen. Prayer boxes made broad.
The uppermost rooms at feasts. The best seats. Greetings in the markets, "and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi."
The crowd might expect him to tell them to stop listening to those teachers. He doesn't. And then he turns, and the warning lands on his own friends.

teach.b: "The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not." He honors the teaching.
What he names is a gap, between saying and doing, and a hunger to be seen. Then he faces the disciples.
"But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren." Call no man on earth your father, he says; one is your Father, in heaven.
One teacher, and everyone else on the same level, brothers and sisters, nobody above the rest. Churches read the title part differently.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians call their priests Father and hear a warning about pride, not a ban on a word. Other churches prefer plain names for their ministers.
Then the line that flips the ladder: "he that is greatest among you shall be your servant."
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Greek word for servant there is diakonos, the word churches later used for deacons. The title itself means the one who serves.

teach.h: THE GREATEST SHALL BE YOUR SERVANT.
teach.b: And the chapter's rule runs both ways: "whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted."

how: Some churches use titles such as Father or Reverend and some prefer plain names; both read Matthew 23 as a check on pride in whoever leads, and deacons in some churches take their name from the Greek word for servant.

games.q: your older cousin gives great advice about saving money, then blows his paycheck every weekend. by Matthew 23:3, what do you do with his advice?
o: keep the good advice, and don't copy the spending.
ignore all of it: a hypocrite's words don't count.
copy him: if he says it, he must live it too.
games.why: Jesus says of the teachers in Moses' seat: whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works. the teaching stands; the gap is the warning.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one title you like to wear: the smart one, the oldest, the boss, the one who is always right. Draw one line through it, and under it write the one word Jesus gives everyone who follows him: brethren.
Keep the paper in your open hand while you breathe, and let the crossed-out title stay crossed out.

wordCard.voice: One teacher. Jesus' word on titles in Matthew 23: one master over all, and everyone else brethren.

orig.note: Greek for servant in Matthew 23:11, the word churches later used for deacons.

carryVoice: Keep this: the greatest serves, and even the word for deacon means it. See you tomorrow.
